title: Cap. IX Arg. 13 Sol: 'absolutely' does not mean without means — God provides for means and end; effects arise freely and contingently (Aquinas; Paul 1 Cor. ix. 27)
pass_a_gloss: Nor does that word absolute or precise, which they so often inculcate, help the adversaries at all. For God is said absolutely to have predestined, and absolutely to will to save the predestined, not that without any means to be applied, or any conditions to be fulfilled on the part of men, he wills to save the same, but that of his supreme mercy he provides both concerning the means and concerning the end. But concerning both he has so provided, that although the order of predestination is certain, and, it being posited that such a person is predestined, it is impossible that he perish and be damned, yet the effects of predestination are produced according to the condition of the subject, and according to the nature of the proximate causes which Divine providence has ordained unto such effects (as Aquinas says, ibid. art. 6.), that is, freely and contingently. Hence Paul, Rom. viii. 38, who in respect of Divine election and ordination understood that he could not fall from salvation, yet became no whit more sluggish in promoting his own salvation, but bruises his body, and brings it into servitude, lest having preached unto others he himself somehow become a reprobate, 1 Cor. ix. 27. The firmness therefore of Divine election does not make the office of human diligence superfluous, whether in respect of himself or of others.
pass_b_english: That word absolute or precise, which they hammer so often, does the adversaries no good. When God is said absolutely to have predestined, and absolutely to will the predestined's salvation, the point is not that he saves them with no means used and no conditions on men's part fulfilled. It is that of supreme mercy he looks ahead to means and end alike. He has so looked to both that the order of predestination stays certain — and once such a person is predestined, perishing and damnation are impossible — while still the effects of predestination come forth by the subject's condition and by the nature of the near causes providence set for those effects (Aquinas, ibid. art. 6): freely, contingently. So Paul, who with an eye to divine election and ordination knew he could not fall from salvation (Rom. viii. 38), did not grow idle in pressing his own: he bruises his body and brings it under, lest after preaching to others he himself somehow prove a reprobate (1 Cor. ix. 27). Divine election's firmness, then, leaves human diligence no spare office — for oneself or for others.
source_text: Neque quicquam juvat adversarios vocabulum illud, absolute sive praecise, quod toties inculcant. Deus enim dicitur absolute praedestinasse, et absolute velle servare praedestinatos, non quod sine ullis mediis adhibendis, aut ullis conditionibus ex parte hominum implendis, eosdem velit servare, sed quod pro summa sui misericordia tam de mediis quam de fine prospicit. De utrisque autem ita prospexit, ut quamvis ordo praedestinationis certus sit, et, posito quod talis persona praedestinetur, sit impossibile quod pereat et damnetur, tamen effectus praedestinationis producantur secundum conditionem subjecti, et secundum naturam causarum proximarum quas ad tales effectus Divina providentia ordinavit (ut inquit Aquinas, ibid. art. 6.), hoc est, libere et contingenter. Hinc Paulus, Rom. viii. 38, qui respectu electionis et ordinationis Divinae intellexit se non potuisse a salute excidere, tamen nihilo segnior evasit in salute sua promovenda, sed contundit corpus suum, et in servitutem redigit, ne quo modo cum aliis praedicavit ipse reprobus fieret, 1 Cor. ix. 27. Firmitas igitur electionis Divinae non facit ut supervacaneum sit officium diligentiae humanae, sive respectu sui ipsius sive aliorum.
